newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to invite foreigners to monitor election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to invite foreigners to monitor election.

text.p: Indonesia will invite foreigners to monitor the country's general election in May, the Jakarta Post newspaper reported on Saturday.
It would mark the first time foreigners had been invited to observe a national poll during President Suharto's three decades of rule over the mainly Moslem nation.
"We will invite neighbouring countries and foreign countries to monitor the election," Interior Minister Yogie Memet, who also heads the election implementation committee, told reporters on Friday.
Memet did not name the countries to be invited and gave no further details.

A number of international human rights groups are considering sending delegations, probably unofficially, to monitor the May 29 election, which has come under greater scrutiny since the exclusion of a key minority party leader.

Megawati Sukarnoputri, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party's (PDI) former head, was ousted last June at a government-backed congress and replaced by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi in a move which has destabilised the party.
A police raid to evict Megawati supporters from PDI party headquarters on July 27 sparked the worst rioting in Jakarta in 20 years. At least four people died in the violence.
Memet also told journalists to report the poll accurately.
"Just write the facts. Otherwise, foreigners get different and negative impressions of the election process," he said.

The two minority parties, the PDI and Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), have complained about tight restrictions the government has placed on election campaigning, which officially starts on April 29.
The ruling Golkar party won 68 percent of the vote in the last polls in 1992, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent. Golkar is aiming for more than 70 percent in the coming poll.

Authorities arrested three leaders of the unrecognised United Democratic Party of Indonesia (PUDI) on Wednesday in what political analysts said was a crackdown on government critics ahead of the election.
Police have banned street parades and restricted public gatherings, while broadcasts on state television and radio must be checked by government officials before going to air.
The minority parties, which rely almost totally on government funds, have also complained about a lack of money available for campaigning.

They said Golkar, whose leaders include government ministers as well as leading businessmen and children of President Suharto, has no problem with access to funds and its activities receive wide coverage in state media.
